metadata.title: How Blind Journal protects your writing
metadata.description: See how Blind Journal separates authentication from decryption, encrypts journal entries in the browser, and stores only protected records on the server.

hero.title: How Blind Journal protects your writing
hero.body: Blind Journal separates authentication from decryption. Your browser holds the key material needed to open your journal; the server handles accounts, sessions, and encrypted storage. You still get normal sign-in and remote storage without giving the backend the keys required to read your entries.

bigPicture.title: Where does my journal get encrypted?
bigPicture.body: While you read or edit an entry, its plaintext exists in the browser. Before the title or body is sent anywhere, Blind Journal encrypts it locally. The server receives ciphertext instead of the readable entry.
bigPicture.httpsBody: In a typical web app, TLS ends at the server and the application can read the plaintext. Blind Journal sends already-encrypted journal data through that HTTPS connection, so the server still receives ciphertext after transport encryption ends.
bigPicture.httpsLabel: HTTPS protects the trip, not the destination.

authentication.title: How can the server sign me in without being able to read my journal?
authentication.body: When you enter your passphrase, Blind Journal processes it in your browser and derives two independent branches from the same root: one for authentication and one for unlocking journal keys.
authentication.separationBody: Only the authentication branch crosses the network. The server uses it to verify your sign-in, stores a one-way verifier, and creates an opaque session. The journal-unlock branch stays in browser memory. Because the branches are derived for different purposes, the authentication key cannot decrypt journal entries.

saving.title: What happens when I press Save?
saving.body: Each entry is encrypted independently. When you press Save, the browser generates a new random entry key and uses it to encrypt that entry’s title and body.
saving.storageBody: The browser then wraps the entry key with your journal-unlock key material. What leaves the browser is an encrypted envelope: ciphertext, a protected copy of the entry key, the IV and protocol version, plus the minimal metadata needed to store and retrieve the record. The server never receives the plaintext entry or the unwrapped entry key.

visibility.title: What can the server actually see?
visibility.body: Encryption hides the contents of your journal, not the fact that an account or encrypted record exists. Blind Journal keeps this boundary explicit: the server gets the operational data it needs to run the service, but not the secrets required to turn stored records back into readable entries.

observable.identity: Account identity: normalized username, display name, and opaque user ID.
observable.derivation: Key-derivation metadata: account salt and key-schedule version.
observable.authentication: Authentication data: a one-way verifier and hashed session records.
observable.records: Encrypted-record metadata: entry IDs, timestamps, ciphertext sizes, and record counts.
observable.operations: Operational metadata: request timing, IP-derived data, and access patterns.
observable.signIn: During account creation and sign-in: the derived authentication key carried in the request.

private.keyEncryptionKey: The key-encryption key used to unlock entry keys.

zeroKnowledge.title: What does zero knowledge mean here?
zeroKnowledge.body: Here, zero knowledge describes a specific system boundary: the backend can authenticate you, authorize requests, and store your journal without possessing the key material required to decrypt journal content.
zeroKnowledge.limitsBody: It does not mean the server learns nothing. Account identifiers, record sizes, timestamps, request timing, and access patterns remain observable. It also does not mean Blind Journal uses a formal zero-knowledge proof system.
zeroKnowledge.browserBoundary: An unlocked journal is plaintext in your browser. Code running in the same origin could potentially read it. A server compromise that can change the JavaScript delivered to a future browser session is therefore a different threat from a database or backend that merely holds encrypted records. XSS prevention, dependency control, and a restrictive Content Security Policy matter here.
zeroKnowledge.browserBoundaryLabel: The browser is part of the trust boundary.

architecture.title: How does the whole system fit together?
architecture.body: Taken together, the design has four jobs. The browser derives keys and handles plaintext. HTTPS protects traffic while it moves. The server authenticates users, authorizes requests, and manages sessions. The database persists encrypted journal envelopes and observable metadata.
architecture.serverBody: When an entry is opened, the process runs in reverse: ciphertext returns to an unlocked browser, the protected entry key is unwrapped locally, and only then is the journal decrypted. No server-side layer has both the stored record and the key material needed to turn it back into readable content.

technicalDepth.title: Built from established cryptographic primitives
technicalDepth.derivation: Argon2id derives a short-lived 256-bit master key from the passphrase and account salt. HKDF-SHA-256 then derives domain-separated authentication and AES-KW key-encryption material.
technicalDepth.entries: Each entry gets a random 256-bit AES-GCM key and a fresh 96-bit IV. Authenticated additional data binds the encrypted envelope to its protocol version, user, and entry, and the entry key is wrapped before storage.
technicalDepth.body: The design uses standard, widely deployed primitives through libsodium and Web Crypto. The custom part is the protocol that composes them, not the cryptographic algorithms themselves.
technicalDepth.protocol: The key schedule and encrypted-entry format are versioned. Cryptographic operations come from libsodium and Web Crypto, derived CryptoKey objects are non-extractable where possible, and raw key material is kept in memory only as long as practical.

closing.title: Explore the implementation
closing.body: Want to verify the details? The repository documents the protocol, threat boundaries, and implementation behind every claim on this page.
